name: Satellite Imagery
title: Satellite Imagery
answer: Satellite imagery as alternative data covers the use of overhead images to measure physical activity that shows up in economic or environmental indicators. Analysts look at parking lot occupancy at retailers, oil storage tank shadows, crop health, construction progress, shipping traffic, and mining output. It sits alongside other alternative data sets such as credit card transactions and geolocation pings, and it is used by investors, insurers, and supply chain analysts. The field is distinct from traditional remote sensing because the goal is often a tradable signal or a risk metric rather than a scientific map.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Satellite imagery as alternative data covers the use of overhead images to measure physical activity that shows up in economic or environmental indicators. Analysts look at parking lot occupancy at retailers, oil storage tank shadows, crop health, construction progress, shipping traffic, and mining output. It sits alongside other alternative data sets such as credit card transactions and geolocation pings, and it is used by investors, insurers, and supply chain analysts. The field is distinct from traditional remote sensing because the goal is often a tradable signal or a risk metric rather than a scientific map.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of public and commercial satellite constellations, ground stations, and cloud computing. Public programs such as Sentinel and Landsat provide free imagery at moderate resolution, while commercial providers like Planet and Maxar offer higher resolution and tasking. Data flows into cloud storage, often as tiled image archives, and processing pipelines use GPUs or distributed clusters to handle petabytes. Analysts access the results through APIs, dashboards, or geospatial platforms rather than downloading raw scenes.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The pipeline starts with image acquisition, then georeferencing, cloud masking, and atmospheric correction. Models detect objects such as cars, ships, or storage tanks, and change detection algorithms compare scenes over time to flag new construction or harvest activity. Analysts often combine these signals with other data, like weather or shipping records, and validate them against ground truth or company reports. The output is typically a time series or an index that can be fed into a forecasting model.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk around satellite imagery involve licensing terms, national security restrictions, and privacy concerns. Some governments limit the resolution or the locations that can be imaged or distributed, and commercial providers impose contractual limits on redistribution. Provenance matters because analysts need to know when and where an image was taken and whether it has been altered. The site's 222 compliance and regulation pages cover many of these issues, from export controls to data protection rules.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward higher revisit rates, with small satellites and constellations that image the same spot daily or more often. Machine learning is making it easier to extract signals from lower resolution or radar imagery, which works through clouds. Demand is growing for near real time monitoring of supply chains, emissions, and disaster response. At the same time, regulators and the public are paying more attention to privacy and to the concentration of commercial imagery providers.
